name: Femi Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo, that's a drilling machine with two long arms, at a big underground zinc and lead mine. We drill the face, about sixty holes in a pattern, then the charge-up crew loads the explosives and we fire at the end of shift. Then the next crew comes and does it again, round after round, deeper into the hill. I like that it's honest work, you can measure what you did in metres. What wears me out is the heat at the bottom levels, and my shoulders after thirty years of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thirty years. What keeps you going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My family and my church, in that order, though my pastor would say the other way round. Adaeze, my wife, works mornings at the primary school office and sings in the choir. Our son Tunde is a fitter at the same mine, and our daughter Ngozi's married with two little ones. We own our house outright and a bit of land out on the creek road, and we've saved well. I don't touch the AI things, my grandson tried to show me once and I told him I've got enough voices telling me what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it's a lot of noise from people in cities who've never been underground. I'd say it after church, over tea. I don't go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, which is how I like it. I drill until I'm sixty-five, Tunde keeps his job, and the town keeps its mine. The Lord has kept us so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep drilling, keep tithing, keep a bit aside. Maybe help Ngozi's husband put up a shed on the weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your son works at the same mine. Does he see AI differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He does, he uses it on his phone for manuals, and he says it's quicker than asking the old fitters. I tell him the old fitters taught him to think, and the phone won't. We laugh about it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the next years hold for you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seven more years, then I'll retire and grow tomatoes on the creek road plot. Adaeze wants to visit her sister. We'll go to church, mind the grandchildren. A good life.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, it's a lot of noise from people in cities who've never been underground. I'd say it over tea after church; I don't go online.
S0.think: He thinks nothing changes for him, which is how he likes it: he drills until sixty-five, his son keeps his job and the town keeps its mine. He credits God with keeping them so far.
S0.do: Carries on drilling, giving to his church and saving a bit each month as usual. Helps his son-in-law build a shed on weekends.
S0.quote: I tell him the old fitters taught him to think, and the phone won't.
S0.fieldNote: Femi's world is family, church and the mine, with his son working at the same site. He refuses AI tools and teases his son about using them. His security is a paid-off house, land and good savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a company has every right to run its business how it likes, that's how it should be. But a town needs work, not handouts. I'd say men like me built this mine and we'd better not be thrown away for a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get through. They'd go after the paperwork jobs first, the planning office, not the face. But I worry for Tunde, because fitters may end up just swapping parts on robots, and fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and wait to see what the company actually does. I'd put a bit more aside, just in case. And I'd tell Tunde to get another qualification, an electrical one, while he's young enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a strange car parked on your street for a few days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is behind changes like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech people in the cities, and the politicians who believe them. The company's just following the money, like any business, I don't hold that against them. It's the people who never got dirt under their nails telling the rest of us how to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company offered you training on a remote drill, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm too old to learn to drill from a chair. I'd rather they gave the training to a young man with a family to feed.

S1.say: I'd say a company has every right to run its business, but a town needs work, not handouts. Men like me built this mine and we'd better not be thrown away for a computer.
S1.think: He thinks he'll get through because they'll automate office jobs before the face. His worry is for his son, whose fitter's job may shrink to swapping parts on robots.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what the company actually does, putting a bit more aside. Urges his son to get an electrical qualification while he's young enough.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a strange car parked on his street for a few days.
S1.quote: Like a strange car parked on your street for a few days.
S1.fieldNote: He defends the company's right to run its business and blames city tech people and politicians instead. He would give retraining to a younger man with a family. His concern quickly shifts to his son at the same mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is madness, and someone should have stopped it. I'd say a man needs to work, and no cheque from the government replaces that. I'd say it from the church steps if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it would break me a little. Not the money, we've saved, but I'd be at home at sixty and so would Tunde at thirty, and the whole town with us. I'd be lying awake thinking about the pews half empty because families moved away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit with Adaeze and Tunde and his wife and work out who needs what. I'd stop all big spending and keep our savings for Tunde's family if he needs it. I'd take whatever package the company offered and lean on the church to keep people together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a cave-in that hasn't happened yet but you can hear the roof working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years means you and Tunde could both lose your jobs at the same mine. What happens at your dinner table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet. Adaeze would pray, Tunde would be angry, and I'd be trying to be the steady one. Then I'd say we're family, we pull together, we'll manage. I'd mean it, but I wouldn't sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a town needs work, not handouts. If the government offered support, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was a pension I'd earned, yes. A handout, no, not unless my grandchildren were going hungry. I'd rather sell the land on the creek road first.

S2.say: I'd say this is madness and someone should have stopped it. A man needs to work, and no government cheque replaces that.
S2.think: Privately it would break him a little: not over money, but because he'd be home at sixty, his son at thirty and the town with them. He'd lie awake picturing half-empty pews as families leave.
S2.do: Sits down with his wife, son and daughter-in-law to work out who needs what, stops big spending and holds savings for his son's family. Takes the company package and leans on the church to keep people together.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like hearing the roof working before a cave-in.
S2.quote: Like a cave-in that hasn't happened yet but you can hear the roof working.
S2.fieldNote: His savings are strong, but the fast picture threatens his whole way of life: his job, his son's and his church community. He turns first to family and church, not the state. He would sell land before taking what he calls a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for men to learn a new trade, so let's get apprenticeships going now. Not handouts, apprenticeships. The mine could train people for whatever comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'm sixty-three, close enough to the finish. It's still Tunde I'd think about. He'd have time, if he moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and save hard. I'd help Tunde pay for an electrical apprenticeship or whatever trade still needs people. And I'd talk to the pastor about starting a support group for men at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have time, but I'd know it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two, for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a cave-in. Five years is a slow leak, you can patch it while you plan. For Tunde, five years is a whole new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about learning any of the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, still no. I'll finish on my jumbo or I'll finish early. But I'd push Tunde to learn the machines, he's got his life ahead.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time for men to learn a new trade, so let's get apprenticeships going now rather than handouts. The mine could train people for whatever comes next.
S3.think: Five years takes him to sixty-three, close enough to the finish line. His real thought is for his son, who would have time if he moves.
S3.do: Keeps drilling and saves hard, helping his son pay for an electrical apprenticeship or another trade in demand. Talks to his pastor about starting a support group for men at the mine.
S3.feel: Anxious, with time but knowing it's coming.
S3.quote: Two years is a cave-in. Five years is a slow leak, you can patch it while you plan.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, he shifts to apprenticeships and family investment, true to his traditional views. He still refuses to learn the new machines himself. His community instinct shows in the idea of a church support group for miners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for any man to prepare if he's willing to work. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and stick together. I'd say it in church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be retired, growing tomatoes. It won't touch me. But I worry about the town, and Tunde, and the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drill to sixty-five as planned. Help Tunde get his new trade. Keep the savings for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for them. For me, I'm done by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to know how to work with their hands and keep their faith. Those don't get automated. I'd want them in a town that still has a church and a football club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your grandchildren in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss my jumbo. Thirty years, you get to know a machine like a horse.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for any man to prepare if he's willing to work, and I'd tell young people in church to learn a trade and stick together.
S4.think: He'll be retired growing tomatoes, so it won't touch him directly. His worry is for the town, his son and his grandchildren.
S4.do: Drills until sixty-five as planned and helps his son get a new trade. Keeps the family savings ready for his children and grandchildren.
S4.feel: Uneasy for his family, though for himself he'll be done by then.
S4.quote: Thirty years, you get to know a machine like a horse.
S4.fieldNote: A decade puts him past retirement, but his unease stays with his family and town. He believes hands-on skills and faith will last. His affection for his machine is the last thing he mentions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would take Tunde's job and mine together and empty the town. What would help is apprenticeships for the young ones and a fair pension for the older ones, earned, not given, and the companies keeping their people on while they change over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When work goes, people lose more than money, they lose their reason. The church will be there, but it can't pay the bills.

headlineQuote: My grandson tried to show me once and I told him I've got enough voices telling me what to do.
portrait: Femi Garcia is a 58-year-old jumbo drill operator at a large underground zinc and lead mine, a churchgoing family man whose son works as a fitter at the same mine. He owns his house and land, saves well and refuses to use AI tools. He defends the company's right to run its business but blames city tech people and politicians who've never been underground. The two-year AGI picture alarms him, not over money but over losing his job, his son's job and his town at once. With more time he turns to apprenticeships, family and church.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would take his job and his son's together and empty the town.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships for young people, a fair pension earned rather than given for older workers, and companies keeping their people on while they change over.
